header:
Date: 2025-09-12
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Li (Redwood SRE), Dana Ortiz (Atlas Head of ML), Ravi Patel (Atlas Infra), Maya Chen (Atlas Security), Oliver Grant (Atlas Product)
summary: Deep technical troubleshooting session focused on frequent OOMs and intermittent CUDA errors during high-concurrency inference runs. Covered KV cache behavior, batching strategies, memory fragmentation, quantization tradeoffs, retry semantics and recommended observability artifacts. Agreed next steps: run Redwood stress harness, exchange driver/kernel logs, share repro, test on Dedicated with tuned batching and quant profile.
topics: OOM root causes (fragmentation, workspace, batch peaks)
KV cache eviction and resume behavior
Observability data to collect (nvprof, syslogs, allocator traces)
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex (Redwood): ok thanks everyone for making time, quick intro - i'm alex from redwood, priya and tom are with me.  
[00:00:12] Dana (Atlas): thanks, we appreciate it. we wanted to do a deep dive on the OOMs we've been seeing in staging and a couple of timeouts in prod.
[00:00:20] Priya (Redwood): great, can you give a quick symptom summary? are OOMs tied to specific endpoints or seq lengths?
[00:00:28] Dana: mostly long-context chat endpoints, anything above about 8k tokens. sometimes it happens during spikes — high qps with mixed short and very long requests.
[00:00:37] Ravi (Atlas): to add, we saw CUDA out-of-memory in the logs but sometimes the processes crash with cublas errors, and then our orchestrator retries which makes the tail worse.
[00:00:47] Tom (Redwood): okay that lines up with memory fragmentation + transient workspace needs. does your staging cluster use preemptible instances or ephemeral GPUs?
[00:00:56] Ravi: yes some nodes are preemptible spot instances in staging. prod is on reserved, but we've seen similar timeouts there too.
[00:01:02] Priya: two immediate suspects: 1) combined peak memory usage from batching + KV cache for long contexts (kv cache for 8k tokens is big), and 2) workspace allocations for certain kernels that expand with sequence length.
[00:01:15] Oliver (Atlas): what about our quantized models — we pushed an int8 build last week — could that be related?
[00:01:22] Priya: possibly. quantization reduces weight size but can increase workspace in some kernels or change kernel selection, which changes memory patterns. there can also be alignment/pinning differences.
[00:01:31] Dana: we saw that OOMs are more frequent when we enable batching with max_batch 64. with smaller batch sizes it's rarer but throughput drops.
[00:01:40] Alex: classic latency vs cost tradeoff. we'll talk tuning, and also retry semantics — we need to avoid retry storms.
[00:01:46] [00:02:00] Priya: can you share the error snippet you have? the cublas message or cuda stack?
[00:02:06] Ravi: sending it in chat but here's a paste: 
"cuda runtime error (2): out of memory at /workspace/src/runtime.cu:412"
and sometimes "cuDNN_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED" or truncated kernel errors.
[00:02:22] Tom: those stack messages are useful. two angles to collect: allocator traces (jemalloc or cudaMalloc logs), and kernel workspace reports. nvprof/nvtx traces help to see which kernel spikes memory at the failure moment.
[00:02:36] [00:03:00] Priya: also, we should look at fragmentation. long-lived allocations like KV cache can fragment device memory so occasional large temporary workspaces can't be satisfied even if total free memory appears sufficient.
[00:03:12] Dana: is there a way to prioritize eviction or reserve headroom per node? we've got mixed-request profiles so one big request ruins others.
[00:03:21] Priya: yes, two things — one is conservative per-request budgeting: cap max_seq_len or apply server-side truncation or partial K/V materialization. second, Redwood supports reservation of a per-GPU headroom and admission control: requests that would exceed headroom are rejected early with 429 rather than causing OOM.
[00:03:39] Ravi: we actually saw retries from client side when 429s return, and that created a retry storm.
[00:03:45] Alex: that points to retry semantics — Atlas client currently retries on 429? we usually recommend idempotency tokens and exponential backoff with jitter; also distinguishing retryable error codes (5xx, transient) vs resource-limit 4xx.
[00:03:57] Maya (Atlas): from security side, we want to keep logs for audit—what logs do you need? we can't share everything but we can provide driver versions, nvml logs, and selected core dumps.
[00:04:07] Tom: that should be enough to start. specifically: NVIDIA driver version, CUDA runtime version, libcudnn version, output of nvidia-smi -q before/after, and the stderr of the failed process. if possible nvprof traces and allocator traces.
[00:04:20] [00:05:00] Priya: another thing: batching strategy. If you do synchronous batching with dynamic batch sizing, peaks can be large. Redwood's runtime has continuous batching that tries to maintain latency SLOs by trimming batch depth for requests marked latency-sensitive. Do you mark priorities?
[00:05:13] Dana: we tag some routes as low-latency but many teams call the same endpoint and no priority is propagated.
[00:05:19] Priya: recommend two quick mitigations: 1) set max_batch lower for high-memory routes, 2) enable prefix-KV caching to reduce recomputation for streaming chats.
[00:05:30] Oliver: quick question on KV cache: when a request times out and is retried, does the server reallocate a new KV cache or can it resume? we're seeing doubled memory when retries come in.
[00:05:40] Tom: Redwood's default behavior currently allocates per-request KV state; if a retry comes in as new request it will allocate again. We have an optional 'resume_key' flow where client supplies an idempotency/resume token and we can attempt to attach the same KV cache when available to avoid duplication — but it depends on your client being able to pass that token.
[00:06:00] Priya: also note eviction policies — our runtime uses LRU-ish per-GPU small-object eviction but large contiguous KV blocks are harder to evict quickly. so we prefer prefix compression and truncated KV for very long contexts.
[00:06:12] [00:06:45] Ravi: about the CUDA errors — could driver/kernel mismatches cause intermittent cuDNN alloc failures? we recently updated drivers.
[00:06:52] Tom: yes mismatches or incompatible cudnn can change kernel selection and memory behavior. also some driver versions have known memory leak bugs. that's why we ask for exact nvml/nvidia-smi and dmesg.
[00:06:59] Dana: we can replicate driver versions across staging and prod.
[00:07:05] Priya: for longer-term fixes: quantization profiles that are correctness-verified and kernel-aware are best. naive int8 can change memory footprint unpredictably; use Redwood's verified quant profiles or test on dedicated to measure workspace changes.
[00:07:20] Oliver: what about offloading KV to CPU or NVMe? we heard about CPU offload and that it hurts latency.
[00:07:26] Priya: offload is a tradeoff — CPU/NVMe reduces GPU footprint at cost of latency. For very long contexts that are cold, offload can be acceptable. For low-latency chat you want KV resident on GPU. We can propose a hybrid: keep recent KVs on GPU, older prefixes offloaded. Redwood has configs for partial materialization.
[00:07:40] [00:08:30] Alex: let's talk about retry semantics in Redwood's runtime — when we retry a failed request, we try to be idempotent but there's complexity with streaming responses and tokens already emitted. In your case, retries triggered by orchestrator restarts cause a new inference run and reallocation. We need to prevent the orchestrator from blind immediate retries.
[00:08:46] Ravi: our kube liveness/restart policy sometimes restarts pods on OOM. do you recommend returning error to client rather than process crash?
[00:08:53] Tom: process crash must be avoided. we recommend the server captures the OOM and returns a 507 or 429 style error instead of letting the OS kill process. that requires allocator hooks and conservative allocations.
[00:09:04] Priya: additionally, enable async eviction hooks — if memory is low, runtime can reject new large requests and let smaller ones through. that's safer than crash+restart.
[00:09:12] Maya: from compliance, we need audit logs of crashes and retries. can those be exported to our SIEM?
[00:09:18] Alex: yes we can stream per-request logs and structured events to your logging endpoint; we will include error codes and allocation footprints.
[00:09:24] [00:10:00] Dana: can we run a targeted test? small repro that simulates k qps with mixed seq lengths?
[00:10:06] Priya: yes we'll provide a stress harness. we'll run two tests: 1) spike of long requests to reproduce OOM, 2) sustained high-qps mixed-profile to observe fragmentation over time. we'll capture nvprof and allocator traces.
[00:10:18] Ravi: what about kernel-level debug? you mentioned nvprof but that's deprecated; nv-nsight-cli?
[00:10:24] Tom: nvprof is end-of-life but it still gives allocation info; nv-nsight and CUPTI provide richer traces. we'll accept any of those. also we can instrument Redwood agent to log allocator stack traces at OOM time.
[00:10:36] [00:11:00] Oliver: i wanted concrete config suggestions we can try quickly.
[00:11:04] Priya: suggested quick config: max_batch 16 for long-context routes; per-GPU headroom reserve 10% for workspace; enable 'resume_key' token on clients; set retry policy to exponential backoff with max_retries=2 and jitter; mark latency-sensitive routes with priority=high so continuous batching trims them.
[00:11:22] Alex: also suggest enabling quant_profile conservative (reduces kernel workspace) rather than aggressive int8 until we validate.
[00:11:28] Dana: noted.
[00:11:35] [00:12:00] Ravi: for Dedicated testing, any advice on GPU types or driver versions?
[00:12:06] Tom: A100 40GB or 80GB reduces OOMs for 8k contexts; if you must use 80GB you have more headroom. driver wise, recommend CUDA 12.x and matching cuDNN; we'll share our validated matrix.
[00:12:19] Priya: we also recommend enabling MPS for mixed workloads when multiple small models share a GPU — it helps packing but has tradeoffs with isolation.
[00:12:30] Maya: ok from security side, we'll only share curated logs; is that enough?
[00:12:35] Tom: yes curated nvml, driver info, and stderr should be sufficient to start.
[00:12:40] [00:13:00] Alex: let's capture a follow-up plan: Priya runs stress tests and shares traces; Ravi provides repro and config; we'll schedule a follow-up in 1 week to run a dedicated test.
[00:13:12] Dana: sounds good.
[00:13:20] [00:30:00] (Transcript abridged — technical exchange continued, Priya walked through flamegraph examples and allocation timelines. Highlights:)
[00:30:12] Priya: observed pattern in similar customers: repeated mid-run ephemeral allocations - often from attention kernels - cause fragmentation; best fix is a combination of headroom reservation + limit per-request kv allocation + trimming batch depth dynamically.
[00:30:45] Ravi: is there a risk that reserving headroom will reduce throughput too much?
[00:30:50] Priya: depends on percent. 8-12% headroom often prevents catastrophic OOMs while keeping most throughput. we can tune.
[00:31:10] Tom: we recommended collecting per-request mem histograms; Redwood agent can emit those.
[00:31:20] [00:45:00] (More discussion about retry semantics and idempotency tokens, with example curl flows and headers).
[00:45:12] Priya: example header: X-Resume-Key: <uuid> — if client supplies this we try to reattach KV state within a grace window (default 30s). if the original request completed partially and tokens were streamed, we ensure dedup by correlating stream ids.
[00:45:35] Oliver: what about billing or cost implications for keeping KV around?
[00:45:40] Alex: keeping KV cached has cost; for Dedicated you can configure retention windows and eviction policies. for hosted we have tiered retention options. we'll include sample cost math.
[00:45:52] [00:55:00] (Tom discussed diagnostics to capture: allocator stacks, cuda-memcheck, kernel workspace sizes. Priya showed a small repro where sequence length + batch spikes OOM.)
[00:55:10] Priya: in the repro the failure happens at token step ~2200, where a high-memory matmul kernel allocates temporary workspace that pushes allocation over free threshold. after fragmentation you see smaller allocations fail too.
[00:55:25] Ravi: is there anything we can change in tokenizer or model config to reduce kv size?
[00:55:30] Priya: reducing kv precision (float16 -> int8) reduces size but could change kernels; better approach: prefix summarization (truncate or summarize older context) and sparse attention for prefixes if model supports it.
[00:55:44] [01:05:00] (Wrap up and recap)
[01:05:10] Alex: recap of agreed actions and configs: stress harness run, share traces, enable shorter max_batch for long-context routes, set retry policy and idempotency tokens, test on Dedicated with conservative quant profile and 10% headroom.
[01:05:26] Dana: we'll get the repro to you by monday.
[01:05:30] Alex: great thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invite for the test and share the Redwood stress harness link + docs.
[01:05:40] Priya: thanks all.
[01:05:45] Maya: thanks.
[01:05:50] (call ends)
